steps.narration: Are your clients complaining their site doesn't look right on their Google Nest Hub? Or their child's Tamagotchi?
In the old days, the Block Grid gave each block one layout. To make it responsive, you did it yourself, in CSS.
Usually by stuffing framework classes into the area alias. Which is not what an alias is for.
Here's a block on a tablet. The badge says we're using the six column layout. Area D is first, then A, then B and C. Oh dear. That's not the order the client wanted.
So let's open the block's Areas tab in the backoffice. Under Layouts, here's the six column layout, drawn to scale.
To change the order, I drag area A by its handle and drop it on area D. Watch the Order numbers. A is now one, and D is two.
The client also wants B bigger. I grab its bottom right corner and drag it across. It snaps to the grid, and its Columns number goes from three to six.
Submit, and save the data type.
Back to the tablet, and refresh. A is first, D is second, and B now spans the full width. No CSS touched.
Now the phone. In the three column layout, I drag area D by its handle and drop it on area C, so D comes first. Save again.
On the phone, D now leads the page. Different orders and different sizes, on every screen.
One block, four layouts. Big screen. Laptop. Tablet. Phone. Or quite possibly, a Tamagotchi.
No CSS framework required. Aliases go back to being names. Responsive Areas.
